articles.summary: El campeón Olympiacos, Panathinaikos, Real Madrid y Fenerbahce, los grandes favoritos
articles.body: La Euroliga más emocionante y abierta de la historia arranca este jueves con el Olympiacos, vigente campeón, encabezando la lista de favoritos como principal candidato para revalidar el título, seguido por un puñado de equipos que se han reforzado mucho como Panathinaikos, Fenerbahce o Real Madrid, que presentó su candidatura al título conquistando de forma brillante la primera edición de la Supercup de la Euroliga. Un peldaño más abajo aparecerían otros equipos muy potentes y bien armados como Hapoel Tel Aviv, Barcelona, Dubai Basketball, Anadolu Efes o Valencia. De ese ramillete de equipos, sin descartar otros aspirantes, deberían salir los cuatro equipos que disputarán la Final Four, que esta temporada se celebrará en el Etihad Arena de Abu Dabi (Emiratos Árabes Unidos), que acaba de acoger la SuperCup, del 28 al 30 de mayo. La competición seguirá contando esta temporada con 20 equipos con la novedad del Besiktas, que ocupará la plaza del AS Monaco como subcampeón de la Eurocup, tras renunciar el campeón de la segunda competición, el JL Bourg francés. Será la última campaña con 20 equipos antes de que se produzca la ampliación a 24 equipos prevista para la campaña 2027-28, por lo que volverán a disputarse 38 jornadas de temporada regular antes del los Play-In y los playoffs de cuartos de final de los que saldrán los cuatro clubes que jugarán la Final Four. Los equipos que lleguen más lejos en la competición podrían llegar a disputar casi un centenar de partidos sumando los que jueguen en sus Ligas nacionales, por lo que se han reforzado considerablemente en número para resistir tanto desgaste. Se lleva la palma el Hapoel Tel Aviv con 22 jugadores en plantilla, seguido por Estrella Roja (19), Dubai (19), Real Madrid (17) y Anadolu Efes (17). En total entre las 20 plantillas suman 305 jugadores, una media de 15,2 por equipo, aunque oficialmente sólo pueden inscribir 12 jugadores en el acta de los partidos, por lo que los entrenadores tendrán que analizar bien los descartes para cada jornada. Y son muchos los jugadores nuevos, con un total de 150 fichajes, lo que significa que el 49,3% del total de cada equipo serán caras nuevas. Además, hasta nueve equipos estrenan entrenador esta temporada, cinco de ellos españoles: París Basketball (Maxime Lefevre), Estrella Roja (Ibon Navarro), Dubai Basketball (Xavi Pascual), Bayern Munich (Anton Gavel), ASVEL Villeurbanne (Tony Parker), Panathinaikos (Zeljko Obradovic), Real Madrid (Pedro Martínez), Valencia (Xavi Albert) y Virtus Bolonia (Álex Mumbrú). articles.title: NBA Training Camps 2026 Start Dates, Schedules and Top Storylines to Watch
articles.summary: The 2026 NBA offseason produced an unforgettable wave of landscape-shifting player movement.
articles.body:
The 2026 NBA offseason produced an unforgettable wave of landscape-shifting player movement.

The 2026-27 NBA season will determine exactly how much the hoops world changed amid all of that activity.

Before any of that happens, though, teams will soon break for training camp to prepare for the 82-game grind ahead. After providing the starting dates for all 30 of those training camps, we'll spotlight two key storylines that may well shape this entire season.

Detroit Pistons, New York Knicks, Orlando Magic

Atlanta Hawks, Boston Celtics, Brooklyn Nets, Charlotte Hornets, Chicago Bulls, Denver Nuggets, Golden State Warriors, Indiana Pacers, Los Angeles Clippers, Los Angeles Lakers, Memphis Grizzlies, Miami Heat, Milwaukee Bucks, Minnesota Timberwolves, New Orleans Pelicans, Oklahoma City Thunder, Philadelphia 76ers, Phoenix Suns, Portland Trail Blazers, Sacramento Kings, San Antonio Spurs, Toronto Raptors, Utah Jazz, Washington Wizards

Who Can Challenge the Champs in New-Look East?

The reigning champion New York Knicks should, by default, be granted the top spot on the Eastern Conference pecking order. But after so many impact additions were made around them, who has a legitimate chance of dethroning the champs?

The star-studded Philadelphia 76ers come first to mind after supplementing their Tyrese Maxey-Joel Embiid foundation with the summer arrivals of Jaylen Brown and LeBron James. They will, however, have to strike the right offensive balance to keep everyone involved and engaged, and they figure to have some availability issues at some point.

The Cleveland Cavaliers have an argument, especially if new swingman Peyton Watson hits the ground running. They also have the same logistical issues to tackle come playoff time. The Detroit Pistons are another option, though the lack of a second shot-creator to pair with Cade Cunningham is notable (as is the still unsettled restricted free agency of Jalen Duren).

Maybe the return of Kawhi Leonard vaults the Toronto Raptors into the conversation. Perhaps the Miami Heat get there after reeling in their long coveted whale Giannis Antetokounmpo. The Atlanta Hawks could continue their ascension. The Boston Celtics are almost always a factor. And don't discount what the Indiana Pacers might do with a healthy Tyrese Haliburton back at the helm.

The potential threats are numerous—even the Washington Wizards have a case for being the NBA's biggest curiosity—but will any of them rise to championship-level? Stay tuned.

Is Another Spurs-Thunder Showdown Inevitable?

All throughout last season, it felt as if the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder were on a collision course to meet in the Western Conference finals. And that's exactly how things transpired with the Spurs ultimately escaping a seven-game thriller in the postseason's penultimate round.

The Spurs effectively return their entire rotation with another veteran shot-maker added to the mix (Tobias Harris). And while the Thunder made a few financially driven cuts (Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe), but the foundation of their 2025 title team all remains in place.

These two will (and should) snag the top two spots on any Western Conference power ranking you'll find. So, should fans expect another pre-title-round clash? Probably, but few things in sports are ever cemented this early.

While injuries forever loom as any singular team's biggest threat, there are some external challengers who could make it interesting.

The Denver Nuggets will be a factor as long as Nikola Jokić is manning the middle. The Minnesota Timberwolves could prove as potent as ever with LaMelo Ball joining Anthony Edwards in the backcourt. The Houston Rockets might see missing-piece impact from a healthy Fred VanVleet. The Los Angeles Lakers have a super-potent perimeter pairing with Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves, plus Walker Kessler to protect the paint now. The Golden State Warriors are always interesting by virtue of rostering Stephen Curry, and they should get a big boost from a midseason Jimmy Butler return.

In the end, though, the Thunder and Spurs are collective favorites for a reason. If they don't wind up wrestling in the WCF again, it feels more likely that would stem from their own shortcomings as opposed to anything happening around them.

articles.title: Chris Spatola Dies at 47, Mike Krzyzewski's Son-In-Law Was ESPN CBB Analyst
articles.summary: Chris Spatola, a former assistant coach on Mike Krzyzewski's staff at Duke and ESPN college basketball analyst, has died at the age of 47.
articles.body:
Chris Spatola, a former assistant coach on Mike Krzyzewski's staff at Duke and ESPN college basketball analyst, has died at the age of 47.

ESPN issued a statement about Spatola in the wake of his death:

"Chris Spatola brought a unique perspective to ESPN's college basketball coverage, shaped by his experiences as a student-athlete, Army veteran, coach and broadcaster. He was thoughtful, prepared and passionate about the sport, earning the respect of colleagues, coaches, players and fans alike. We extend our heartfelt condolences to his loved ones during this difficult time."

Spatola, who was also the son-in-law to Krzyzewski after marrying his daughter, Jamie Krzyzewski Spatola, in 2004, worked on the Blue Devils staff from 2007 to 2012.

He won a national title as part of the 2009-10 team that defeated Butler in the championship game.

Spatola went to college and played basketball at Army where he was a four-year starter from 1998 to 2002. He ranks in the top 10 in program history in career points (1,543).

Following his graduation, Spatola served five years in the United States Army from 2002 to '07 before going to work at Duke. Krzyzewski also brought Spatola on as a court coach for Team USA during the 2008 Olympics and 2010 FIBA World Championship.

Spatola was hired as a college basketball analyst in 2015.

articles.title: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.summary: Gary Trent Jr.'s new contract raised some eyebrows around the league.
articles.body:
When the Milwaukee Bucks agreed to sign Gary Trent Jr. to a four-year, $64 million deal in July, red flags went up all around the league's office. Days later, reports emerged suggesting the NBA was looking into the signing , though details of the league's probe were scarce.

The league apparently found enough that it decided to launch a full-on investigation , according to The Athletic. The focus of that investigation: whether the Bucks used the contract as a way to circumvent the NBA salary cap.

The league reportedly hired law firm Hecker Fink to perform that investigation.

That particular accusation should sound familiar, as the league just wrapped an investigation on the Los Angeles Clippers and Kawhi Leonard that looked into the exact same thing. While both teams were accused of the same violation, their methods for allegedly circumventing the salary cap differ.

In the Clippers' case, the team was accused of using a team sponsor to funnel additional funds to Leonard as a way to get around NBA rules. Accusations surrounding the Bucks are far more straight forward.

The league is reportedly looking into whether the Bucks made handshake agreements with Trent to sign lesser deals the past two offseasons with the promise of Trent eventually receiving a much larger contract this offseason.

The issue stems from Trent's massive pay increase this offseason. After making $2.6 million with the Bucks in 2024 and $3.7 million in 2025, Trent's new deal will pay him an average of over $15 million the next four years.

That massive pay increase came after Trent experienced a down season, one in which he averaged just 8.1 points per game, his lowest scoring output since his rookie season.

When reached for comment by The Athletic, the NBA, Bucks and Trent's agency — Klutch Sports — all declined comment. Both the Bucks and Klutch are reportedly working with the NBA as it performs its investigation, per The Athletic.

Should the NBA determine the Bucks purposefully engaged in salary-cap circumvention, the team could see a similar punishment to the Clippers. The NBA came down hard on Los Angeles , docking the team five future first-round picks , fining and suspending team owner Steve Ballmer and fining Leonard.

articles.title: College basketball world mourns Chris Spatola's death: 'All-time great dudes'
articles.summary: Chris Spatola was 'one of the all-time great dudes.' Here's how college basketball is mourning the loss of the ESPN analyst, who died Sept. 21:
articles.body:
ESPN analyst Chris Spatola , 47, unexpectedly died on Monday, Sept. 21, leaving the college basketball world heartbroken.

Spatola, who ranks 10th on Army's all-time scoring list, deployed in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom from 2002-07 following his four-year playing career. He returned to college basketball as a staff member at Duke under his father-in-law Mike Krzyzewski, one of the sport's greatest coaches, from 2007-12 before becoming a broadcaster.

"Chris Spatola brought a unique perspective to ESPN's college basketball coverage, shaped by his experiences as a student-athlete, Army veteran, coach and broadcaster," ESPN said in a statement. "He was thoughtful, prepared and passionate about the sport, earning the respect of colleagues, coaches, players and fans alike. We extend our heartfelt condolences to his loved ones during this difficult time."

It's clear Spatola meant a lot to numerous people in the industry. Those who knew him called him "kind," "egoless" and "an all-time dude" in tributes on social media.

Here are some of those tributes to Spatola:

College basketball, media world mourn Chris Spatola's death

Steve Kornacki, known for election day coverage for NBC, offered interesting perspective on Spatola's path to broadcasting. He said he hadn't seen him in years, but was always touched by what Spatola accomplished.

"This is just shocking," Kornacki wrote. "I grew up with Chris and while I hadn't seen him in a very long time, I was so impressed over the years watching all that he became and achieved in life. He had to be the best basketball player to come through our small town and it was obvious back then he was going places. The kid I remember was friendly and warm and funny and great to talk to and also unusually smart and ambitious. And he put it all together in life.

"Just a huge, total success story who I know made a lot of people from his Groton-Dunstable Middle School days proud. RIP to him and deepest sympathies to his loved ones and many friends."

ESPN play-by-play broadcaster Mike Monaco worked college basketball games with Spatola over the years, saying he was lucky to know him.

"Shocked and devastated to hear the news about Chris," Monaco wrote. "Just keep staring at the screen. Simply a damn good human being. Smart, witty, curious, principled, and kind. And man did he love his family. Praying hard for his family & all those lucky enough to know him."

Numerous tributes noted Spatola's love for his family, including Baylor coach Scott Drew, who called him a "great friend."

"Chris was a friend and someone I really respected," Drew said. "So many Great Memories of Baylor Games he announced. He often talked about his family and I know how much he loved them. Praying for the Spatola Family."

articles.title: Varapalo para el Unicaja: Tyson Pérez apunta al quirófano
articles.standfirst: El hispano-dominicano estará varios meses de baja por un problema en el pie izquierdo
articles.summary: El hispano-dominicano estará varios meses de baja por un problema en el pie izquierdo
articles.body: El Unicaja afronta la semana del estreno en la Liga Endesa con malas noticias en el apartado físico. Txus Vidorreta ha pasado por los micrófonos de Zona Verde, en 101TV, para repasar la actualidad del conjunto cajista y ha confirmado que Tyson Pérez apunta a una baja de varios meses. El técnico bilbaíno también se ha referido a la situación de Tyler Kalinoski, cuyo proceso de recuperación está siendo más lento de lo esperado y que todavía no ha realizado trabajo de contacto durante la pretemporada. A ello se suma la baja de Yannick Nzosa, que estará varios meses apartado por una fractura en el quinto metatarsiano de su pie izquierdo. Y el siguiente en pasar por la enfermería, salvo giro inesperado, será Tyson Pérez. El hispano-dominicano fue infiltrado este martes y este miércoles estaba previsto que se probara en una nueva sesión de trabajo para comprobar su evolución. Sin embargo, las sensaciones no son positivas. La posibilidad de que tenga que pasar por quirófano gana fuerza y, en ese caso, el jugador se perdería varios meses de competición. "En el caso de Tyson Pérez, independientemente de lo que ocurra con la última infiltración que se hizo ayer, hay malas noticias. Es casi seguro que tenga que pasar por quirófano y tenga que estar muchos meses de baja", explicó Vidorreta. El problema no es nuevo para Tyson Pérez. El jugador ya sufrió una lesión similar en el pie derecho la pasada temporada, cuando estuvo dos meses de baja y pudo recuperarse mediante un tratamiento conservador. Ahora las molestias han aparecido en el otro pie y el tratamiento no está dando los resultados esperados. "Tengo un pequeño hueso que me ha salido en el calcáneo y es el que me está dando molestias en el pie izquierdo. No es nada muscular ni físico que puedas decir que si lo trabajas, lo arreglas. He trabajado en el verano como el que más, pero no he tenido los mejores resultados. Estamos intentando todo lo posible para estar bien", explicó el propio Tyson Pérez a los micrófonos de Radio MARCA Málaga.

articles.title: Steph Curry Reveals He Had 'Crazy Blurred Vision' Due to Eye Condition During Warriors' Dynasty
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors star point guard Stephen Curry was too busy winning MVP awards and NBA championships to notice that his eyesight was deteriorating.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors star point guard Stephen Curry was too busy winning MVP awards and NBA championships to notice that his eyesight was deteriorating.

While speaking to Natasha Dye of People , Curry revealed that he was dealing with poor vision at the height of the Warriors' dynasty.

"It was 2018, and I didn't know I was really dealing with crazy blurred vision or distorted images — it was just the way that I saw things, and we compensated around it," Curry said.

By then, Curry was already a two-time NBA MVP on his way to his third championship out of four career titles. However, former Warriors general manager Bob Myers noticed something was off with the sharpshooter while watching a road game broadcast, so he reached out.

"He texted me after the game because apparently the telecast kept showing me when I was on the bench, and he was like, 'You're just squinting, looking like you couldn't see anything. Have you gotten your eyes checked? You should probably go do that because that wasn't normal,'" Curry recalled.

Curry met with an optometrist shortly after speaking to Myers, and while he initially "thought it was going to be nothing," he learned that he was dealing with something serious.

"They told me that I had a rare condition called Keratoconus, the irregular-shaped cornea that obviously leads to blurriness, distorted images," he said. "What I found out about it was it's a progressive condition that can deteriorate your vision over time and it's irreversible if it goes in the wrong direction."

The 38-year-old said he now gets his eyes checked every six months and has become a "trained professional" at putting in his contacts. He added that he's worked with Glaukos to get on a treatment plan that's "curbed all the anxiety around where this could head." Still, he admitted that it took some time to get used to wearing contacts during games.

"That first year or two, and that was me being stubborn at that time because it was a part of my job to be able to see the rim, see the court, even if it was blurry. I was like, 'I'm used to this,'" he said. "But to that point about wearing the contacts, finding the right fit and the right prescription, ones that stayed stable while I was playing."

While he achieved massive success while playing with poor vision earlier in his career, Curry acknowledged that he "can only imagine" what his eyesight would be today if he hadn't listened to Myers' advice.

"It's more that transformation has helped a lot, just give me peace of mind, clarity and help performance in a way that it's not going to tell me I can shoot better, but it just gives me a little bit more energy knowing I can see," he said.

Curry added that he considered overcoming poor eyesight the defining story of his legendary career.

"I joke that when I'm all done, my memoir should be called The Whole Time I Couldn't See ," he said with a laugh.

articles.title: Knicks' Josh Hart Jokes About His Ranking on ESPN's List of Top 100 NBA Players for 2026-27 Season

articles.body:
New York Knicks star Josh Hart has never been shy about poking fun at himself, so he's not sweating his ranking among the best players in the NBA.

After ESPN unveiled its list of the top 100 players entering the 2026-27 season and ranked Hart at No. 89, the 31-year-old laughed off his placement with a funny social media post:

Hart helped lead the Knicks to their first NBA championship since 1973 while serving as the team's do-everything connector and emotional leader. He shot a career-high 41.3 percent from three-point range and averaged 12.0 points, 7.4 rebounds, 4.8 assists and 1.1 steals.

It's safe to say that ESPN's ranking won't change Hart's approach as he tries to help the Knicks defend their title when they open the season on Oct. 20 against the Philadelphia 76ers.

articles.title: Lonzo Ball Denies NBA Retirement Buzz After Discussing His Health, Injury History in Video
articles.summary: Lonzo Ball's injuries have made it difficult for him to play basketball, but he's not looking to retire right now.
articles.body:
Lonzo Ball's injuries have made it difficult for him to play basketball, but he's not looking to retire right now.

On the latest episode of the Ball In the Family podcast (starts 54:00 mark), Ball explained "I feel like I gave everything I had" through his first nine seasons in the NBA.

"I feel like I gave everything I had to hoop, and I feel like everything I got in my life is because of hoop. I'm grateful to even make it to the league and be able to play for nine years," he said.

Ball went on to say he has to "manage" the pain in his knee every day and it swelled up recently when he was playing, but a mix of yoga, stretching and ice makes it "to where I can do s--t" even though it's "still gonna hurt" and it felt like he was "playing on stilts" at times because he can't stop quickly without aggravating it.

Ball's comments led to speculation he may be ready to call it a career, but he confirmed in a post on X that he is still ready for his next opportunity:

The No. 2 pick in the 2017 draft by the Los Angeles Lakers, Ball began having knee issues as a rookie when he sprained his MCL midway through the season.

Ball had arthroscopic surgery to repair his meniscus in July 2018, but he was back for the start of the 2018-19 season. He played in the Lakers' first 47 games before an ankle injury ended his sophomore campaign.

The Lakers traded Ball to the New Orleans Pelicans as part of the Anthony Davis deal. He had arguably the two best years of his career in New Orleans, averaging 13.1 points on 37.6 percent three-point shooting, 6.4 assists and 5.5 rebounds per game in 118 appearances.

Ball went to the Chicago Bulls as a free agent in a sign-and-trade deal with the Pelicans in 2021. This was when the downfall really began due to a torn meniscus early in the year that ended his season.

Knee issues persisted to the point that Ball sat out both the 2022-23 and 2023-24 seasons, including undergoing a cartilage transplant in March 2023 because there was nothing left of his meniscus and it was "bone on bone" in his knee.

Ball returned to game action at the start of the 2024-25 season with the Bulls, but his playing time was often infrequent due to lingering knee issues. He was traded to the Cleveland Cavaliers in July 2025.

After appearing in 35 games with Cleveland, Ball was dealt to the Utah Jazz in February. The Jazz waived him before he played in a game with them.

There haven't been many indications at this point teams are looking at Ball. Last season was the first time in many years he was available on a relatively consistent basis. He played in 35 of Cleveland's first 51 games prior to the midseason trade.

Ball averaged 4.6 points, 4.0 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 1.3 steals per game with the Cavs.

articles.title: Stephen Curry says he wants 'no drama' during season over unresolved extension talks with Warriors
articles.summary: Stephen Curry knows his next contract will have a massive impact on the Warriors.
articles.body:
Stephen Curry has spent his entire 17-year NBA career with the Golden State Warriors . So, when Curry became eligible for a two-year extension with the team in August, it was expected he would quickly sign again and re-up for another couple seasons.

But with training camp on the horizon, Curry has yet to sign a deal with the team. He's taken that track despite the Warriors reportedly giving Curry multiple options to contemplate , per ESPN.

While that uncertainty could cause panic among Warriors fans, Curry said he wants "no drama" to seep into the team if he doesn't sign the extension by the time the season starts, per ESPN.

"I don't want there to be no drama," Curry told ESPN on Wednesday. "No talking points. This team should be competitive and go win."

To further stress that point, Curry said the extension "is going to happen," and that he has an "obvious goal" to stick with the Warriors for the rest of his career. He's currently signed to a one-year, $62.5 million deal for the upcoming season.

Curry — who became eligible for a two-year, $136.7 million max deal in August — will greatly impact the team's cap room depending on what kind of deal he signs. The Warriors are currently projected to have roughly $100 million in cap space available next offseason. If Curry signs for his max, that figure would drop to around $45 million, per ESPN.

But the Warriors can create more flexibility depending on what moves the team makes in the coming months. Curry said that's among his biggest considerations as he waits to sign the extension. At his age — he will be 38 when the 2026-27 NBA season begins — Curry is placing a high emphasis on winning another championship, which could lead to him giving the Warriors more flexibility, as he laid out to ESPN.

"We're in a very interesting situation," Curry said. "All the different salary cap conditions of whether I sign for a max or less or whatever it is, I want to be on a competitive team. I want to have an opportunity to have some flexibility because we haven't had that in years past, the recent past."

Complicating matters is the Warriors' recent performance. While Curry has remained an elite player when healthy, the team missed the playoffs in two of the past three seasons. Curry also battled an injury last season, playing in just 43 games as the team limped to the finish line.

Given those concerns, the Warriors may need to add significant talent next offseason if the team hopes to make one more title run with Curry and Draymond Green . All of that is undoubtedly on Curry's mind as he determines his best path moving forward.

articles.title: The NBA's 5 most interesting newcomers, starring LeBron James, LaMelo Ball and the Lakers' big swing
articles.summary: With media day and training camp just around the corner, let's take a look at a few familiar faces in new places.
articles.body:
With the 2026 NBA offseason now all but concluded, and with media day and training camp just around the corner, it's time to start looking ahead to what's coming next in the NBA.

In that spirit, let's take a look at the five most interesting — to me! — folks who joined a new team this summer.

(We've previously considered my five most interesting: potential free agents in the class of 2027 , comeback players for next season , rising sophomores in the NBA , and veteran extension candidates . That last column included both Giannis Antetokounmpo and Kawhi Leonard, so I won't be writing about them here — although, obviously, they and their new surroundings are both pretty interesting!)

We begin with this really old guy (read: more than two years younger than me) who decided to move to Pennsylvania in search of fame, fortune and a fifth NBA title:

Yes, yes, yes, we all know: There's only one ball. And when a team that already had Joel Embiid (who has, over the course of his career , finished 35.3% of his team's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, turnover or foul drawn) and Tyrese Maxey (average usage rate over the past three seasons : 29%) adds both Jaylen Brown (36.2% usage rate last season, 31% over the past six ) and LeBron James ( 19 seasons north of 30%, 27.2% last season), the lack of a multi-ball option would seem to be at least something of a problem.

Turning a collection of what ESPN's Dean Oliver recently referred to as "super-users" into a harmonious lineup that can elevate the NBA's No. 17 offense last season into a top-tier unit will require sacrifice across the board. But that sacrifice won't be distributed equally; some Sixers are going to need to give up more touches than others.

It probably shouldn't be Maxey, given his elite production as both a pick-and-roll creator and off-ball movement-shooting weapon, his youth, and the likelihood that Nick Nurse would rather gnaw his left foot off than take his All-NBA guard off the floor more often than is medically necessary. I'm more bullish than some on Brown being willing to take a step back from last season's maximalist approach in a new setting — we've certainly seen plenty of evidence that he can contribute at an All-Star level in a superstar timeshare, after all — but the fact that he's a much better play finisher than playmaker suggests that you wouldn't want to tilt his role too far away from shooting and scoring.

Embiid, as ever, remains the most significant variable: how healthy he is and can reasonably stay, how many games and minutes he can actually play, how effectively he can move in space defensively and how comfortably he might be able to navigate life in a reduced role, etc. Generally speaking, though, it's hard to see the most effective employment of Embiid on the offensive end being something besides leveraging his gifts operating out of the post or isolating from the nail — both of which he still does as well as, if not better than, just about anybody in the sport.

Which leaves LeBron : the best passer, most natural playmaker of the bunch, and the player who, despite lapping the entire rest of the squad in laurels and accolades, is likely best suited to reorienting his individual game toward the broader goals of the collective.

(He's also making like $50 million less than the other guys — in salary, anyway — which may or may not matter in discussions like these.)

The most direct path to fitting four "super-users" — plus ascendant sophomore VJ Edgecombe ! — under the same roof is for one of those four to not command a quarter of the team's offensive possessions. James began that during the latter stage of his tenure in L.A., when a Lakers team suddenly featuring offensive engine Luka Dončić and rising star Austin Reaves required some reorganization.

Across parts of two seasons in L.A., when James, Dončić and Reaves shared the floor together, James posted a 23.4% usage rate, according to PBP Stats — significantly below his 28.8% overall mark in those seasons . Narrow it down to just the 2025-26 campaign, and James' usage rate dipped to 21.3% in the minutes the trio shared .

During that March-to-April stretch when the Lakers were rolling, Dončić was getting MVP buzz, and everyone was talking about LeBron suddenly being an overqualified third option ? It dropped all the way down to 19.1% , with James averaging 18.4 points on 55% shooting, 7.4 rebounds, 7.4 assists and nearly 2 blocks-plus-steals per game in that span , with his average time of possession, number of touches, and dribbles and seconds per touch all (slightly) below where they'd been earlier in the season and (significantly) below where they'd been in previous years.

"I know what I'm capable of still doing as an individual, but what's important for this team, I'm able to adapt," James told reporters back in March . "And that's the only thing that matters."

Even approaching age 42, that version of LeBron — the high-efficiency, high-IQ, low-turnover floor-raiser who doesn't need to dominate the ball to elevate others — can thrive in Philly . He can work either end of a pick-and-roll with Maxey and play the high-low game with Embiid. He can sprint the floor in transition with Maxey, Brown and Edgecombe, turning defensive rebounds and turnovers into the kind of easy fast-break buckets the Sixers haven't generated much in the past two seasons .

He can hunt opportunities for duck-ins, back-cuts and drives against closeouts when defenses load to his high-wattage teammates. He can serve as the connective playmaking tissue to turn talented but somewhat disparate parts into a more cohesive and dangerous whole. And when problems arise — and they will, whether in the form of injuries, your-turn-my-turn stagnancy, natural ego-driven friction, or whatever other obstacle emerges when the teeth stop showing and the stomachs start growling — it'll be up to him, the most decorated dude on the Eastern seaboard, to troubleshoot the concerns and get everyone singing from the same hymnal again.

This is the challenge that James set for himself when he assessed the landscape and determined that Philly gave him the best chance to compete for another ring. It's a tall task, and one that's going to demand something radically different from what James has provided throughout the course of his legendary career: not doing more with less, but doing less to provide more.

It's not Kessler's fault the Lakers sent two unprotected first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps to the Utah Jazz for his services. Nor is it his fault that he graciously (I assume) accepted the $130 million contract they offered him to provide those services in L.A. for the next four seasons — top-10 center money for someone who has spent the better part of his NBA career to date far, far away from playing games, minutes or even individual possessions of consequence amid the perpetual rebuild in Salt Lake City.

Now that the picks are sent and the contract's signed, though, it is Kessler's responsibility to carry that burden — the Mikal Bridges Memorial Huge-Pick-Haul-Plus-Nine-Figure-Extension Millstone Around the Neck — as he sets about the work of manning the back line for a Lakers team that has finished league-average or worse in defensive efficiency , and 24th or worse in field-goal percentage allowed at the rim , in four of the last five seasons. And that just saw its best perimeter defender, Marcus Smart , leave for Houston . And that will be fielding lineups with Dončić and the re-signed Reaves — in whose minutes sans Smart the Lakers conceded points at a bottom-10 level last season.

Kessler won't be alone in that effort, of course. A number of the Lakers' other offseason additions — wings Quentin Grimes , Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams , veteran bigs Kevon Looney and Sandro Mamukelashvili — have all shown signs in past stops of being active, positive contributors on the defensive end. Add in holdover chaos agent Jarred Vanderbilt and recent draftees Cameron Carr, Adou Thiero and Bronny James , and head coach JJ Redick might have enough of the bodies and temperament necessary to build the kind of high-motor lineups that have been a hallmark of so many successful teams in recent years.

Since the Jazz drafted him 22nd overall out of Auburn in 2022, Kessler has consistently ranked among the league's premier per-minute rim-runners, rebounders, shot-blockers and interior deterrents. He finished third in Rookie of the Year voting in 2022-23, led the NBA in offensive rebounds per game in 2024-25 (and finished fifth in rebounding overall), has posted top-five finishes in blocks per game three times in four seasons (and he missed nearly all of his fourth season following surgery to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder ), and has the sixth-highest effective field-goal percentage of anybody who's played at least 100 games since entering the league.

In some respects, according to analysis conducted by Iztok Franko , Kessler's defensive metrics compare favorably to the likes of Evan Mobley and Jaren Jackson Jr. — both of whom, you might recall, own Defensive Player of the Year trophies. If he can be the kind of space-eating, mistake-erasing, back-line presence that can cover up for Luka's and Reaves' misdeeds at the point of attack while also providing the sort of "A-list" center production Dončić sought as a pick-and-roll lob threat and board-crashing possession-extender, then Kessler could well live up to the great expectations the Lakers have placed on him; the weight of that millstone gets lighter when you win a ring. ( Just ask Bridges. )

If Kessler can't propel the Lakers above the mountain, though — if they play closer to their mid-40s win total projections and struggle to scratch out wins in one playoff series, let alone the three necessary to get to the Finals? That kind of burden can be awfully heavy to carry around. (At least he'll be well compensated to do it.)

I think Collins — now entering his 10th year in the NBA, which feels like it happened freaking fast — is a perfectly fine player. He's developed into a solid floor-spacing power forward, shooting 39.1% from 3-point range on 4.3 attempts per 36 minutes over the last three seasons , making him one of only a dozen 4/5 types to hit that consistently on that kind of volume in that span. Beyond just the shooting, though, he's a skilled offensive player who can contribute in a number of ways: running the floor in transition, attacking a mismatch in the post, hitting the offensive glass, finding space underneath for cuts and duck-ins, and sometimes serving as a pick-and-roll big who can either dive hard to the rim — something that might not have a ton of utility in Detroit in lineups next to Jalen Duren , but still — or pop to the perimeter, giving defenses something to think about as they try to navigate the manifold unpleasantness that comes with Cade Cunningham bearing down on them.

Collins can shoot (especially from the corners), rebound, play some small-ball 5, run and chew gum at the same time, all while being 6-foot-9 and still sitting on the right side of age 30. (He actually turns 29 on Wednesday. Happy birthday, John.) That Detroit would view that collection of skills and traits to be worth three years and $51 million in free agency seems to be, once again, perfectly fine.

I find myself wondering, though, just how much bringing in Collins to replace Tobias Harris — who got one year and $20 million less to sign with San Antonio — really improves a Pistons team that just stomped its way to 60 wins and won a playoff series for the first time in 18 years, with Harris as its second-leading postseason scorer.

It's possible that Collins, who's more than five years younger than Harris, will be both a better fit for what chief exec Trajan Langdon envisions the Pistons to be and a more productive player than his predecessor in three years' time — an important consideration for a franchise that has to consider how best to construct a roster to compete for titles with Cunningham on a max contract through 2030, Ausar Thompson now on a five-year, $155 million extension and Duren (Detroit hopes) soon sewn up on a sub-max multi-year pact of his own. In that respect, getting Collins on a deal that is non-guaranteed in 2027-28 and 2028-29 to maximize financial flexibility seems like a good piece of business.

It feels at least equally possible, though, that Collins just, y'know, isn't better than Harris. ( Multiple advanced stats certainly suggest that's the case, anyway.) And that a team that was one win away from the conference finals despite Duren being locked in the pain cave for the entirety of the postseason just downgraded in the starting lineup for the purposes of flexibility. And that, by the time next spring rolls around — hey, spring rolls, all right — we find ourselves thinking, "Man, the Pistons' big move really was signing John Collins, huh?"

Maybe we won't. Maybe Detroit's around-the-margins revamping — bringing in Collins, re-signing Kevin Huerter , adding Isaiah Joe , Taurean Prince and Gary Harris — represents a significant enough aggregate addition of shooting and floor-spacing to allow the Pistons' offense to take flight in ways it struggled to at times last season, and particularly in the postseason, when opponents packed the paint against lineups featuring Duren and Thompson, and essentially dared either Cunningham to beat them by himself or for someone else to do something. (You know who was pretty good to have around when that happened? Tobias Harris!) And maybe the Pistons — with a handful of mid-sized salaries, expiring and partially guaranteed contracts , and full control of all of their first-round draft picks moving forward — do finally make that big swing that their fans have been waiting for, pushing their chips in to make a real run at a ring right now.

Maybe, though, Collins winds up looking in Detroit more or less the way he looked in L.A., and Utah, and Atlanta — like a perfectly fine player who doesn't necessarily move the needle when it comes to contention. And maybe, after taking such a dramatic leap forward over the past couple of seasons, the Pistons wind up realizing that "perfectly fine" just isn't quite good enough for where they want to go.

Yes, you read that right: Ja Morant is on Portland now. You would be forgiven if you'd missed that bit of late-June news , or just forgotten about it, considering the two-time All-Star played all of 90 minutes after New Year's Day; while "absence makes the heart grow fonder" is a popular turn of phrase, so is "out of sight, out of mind."

The things that made Morant feel so vital, so electric, so compulsively watchable over his first four NBA seasons — the stuff that led me to once (perhaps a bit too breathlessly!) write that he "leads the NBA in Holy S***, Dude" — were scarcely on display over the last three years in Memphis . Myriad injuries, suspensions and shutdowns have limited Morant to just 79 games in the last three seasons; when he has gotten on the floor, the inconsistent production and largely corrosive vibes he brought with him helped hasten the broader teardown and hoped-for rebuild of the Grizzlies.

More than perhaps any player in the NBA, Morant at his best has existed as an arrow, nocked and loosed directly downhill and aimed at the front of the rim. But the share of his shots that come from point-blank range has declined five years in a row , from nearly half of his total attempts as a rookie in 2019-20 to just 30% in limited action last season ; he also shot 61% on them , his lowest conversion rate since his rookie year.

Combine that with a rising turnover rate and a jumper that has never improved enough to mitigate any decline in up-close effectiveness — of the 255 players who've taken at least 500 3-pointers over the past four seasons, Morant's 29.7% hit rate ranks … 255th — and it's fair to wonder just how much of the exhilarating, explosive, superstar version of Morant we now only vaguely remember is still in there. That the going rate for his services wound up being the balance of Jerami Grant 's underwater-from-the-moment-it-was-signed deal and underwhelming fourth-year forward Kris Murray suggests broad skepticism about how regularly Morant can or will summon that version of himself over the two years and $87 million remaining on his contract .

"There's a growing gap between what Morant is supposed to be and what he's actually been recently," Chris Herrington wrote in the Daily Memphian back in January. "Who can say how those pressures may weigh on him?"

We do have some evidence that it's not gone , though. In the last six games he actually played as a Grizzly, Morant averaged 23.5 points and 9.3 assists in 29.2 minutes per game, driving to the basket 24 times per game , shooting 53.7% from the field (including 74.2% in the restricted area ), 38.9% from 3-point land and 84.2% from the free-throw line on more than six attempts per game.

That included a late-December performance that saw him score 40 points on 16-for-22 shooting against the 76ers, repeatedly dusting VJ Edgecombe and Philadelphia's other perimeter defenders off the bounce and torching Joel Embiid in drop coverage en route to getting pretty much whatever he wanted:

That version of Ja — one that can still get downhill, can still finish on the interior and get to the line, and can still act as an offensive engine — has value, can help a team, and might just be a distressed asset. Which, of course, is music to Tom Dundon's ears .

It's still very much an open question, though, whether a buy-low flyer on a 27-year-old former All-NBA talent can lead to soaring harmonies on this specific Blazers roster.

Lest we forget: Portland will also be welcoming back Damian Lillard , now 36 and coming off a ruptured Achilles tendon, and evidently intends to start him alongside Morant in the backcourt. How can new head coach Micah Nori maintain the spine of last season's near-top-10 defense with two undersized and negative defenders at the point of attack ? Maybe the answer is, " Donovan Clingan and Toumani Camara play like All-Defensive First-Teamers," and maybe, given how they've trended since carving out their places in the league, that's even a pretty decent answer. It's a pretty hard way to live, though — and it's a framework that requires the new-look backcourt paving a pathway to producing more points than it concedes, which comes with its own concerns.

How do Nori and Co. square the likelihood that getting the most out of Morant requires giving him the keys to the offense with the fact that the Blazers were at their best last season with the ball in All-Star wing Deni Avdija 's hands? Can a Portland team that ranked 28th in team 3-point shooting accuracy effectively spread the floor for Morant to be able to attack the rim? (The return of Lillard should help there, at least.)

Beyond that, how does creating enough space in the structure for Morant to soak up his customary star-level usage impact the development of former No. 3 overall pick Scoot Henderson , who started to come on late last season but could still use more seasoning and reps if he hopes to grow into a primary offensive option in a crowded Portland guard room? (Some cold comfort: Losing Shaedon Sharpe to a torn meniscus at least ameliorates some of the competition for minutes, touches and shot attempts in that increasingly crowded backcourt.) Wouldn't it seem to make more sense to bring one of Morant or Lillard off the bench , keeping Jrue Holiday in the starting lineup to better balance the lineups and rotations?

Morant, for his part, told reporters after the trade that he's open to coming off the bench if need be, and that he's excited to play alongside Avdija, Lillard and Holiday, concerns about usage and ball dominance be damned.

"All those guys will most likely unlock new parts of my game, and I'll do the same for them," Morant said . "I don't think it will be a problem having us on the floor or making sure minutes match or anything. We're all very unselfish."

The best intentions of summertime don't always sustain once the temperature starts dropping; if the offense starts to bend away from Morant, as it did late in Taylor Jenkins' tenure in Memphis , it'll be interesting to see how he reacts, and whether he'll be able to find other ways to contribute, and to show the fans in Portland that he really is, as he put it, "a different Ja."

"It's like starting all over again. [...] Over the years, I've grown a lot and learned a lot," he said. "My mindset changed. I go into things differently now. I feel more mature, and I'm ready to work."

The million-dollar question: While the mindset might be different, is Morant physically capable of consistently producing the way he used to? And, if so, does that put Portland in position to push its way up the Western Conference standings back toward serious contention?

Viewed through one lens, the fact that the Wolves took the eventual Western Conference champions to six games in the second round after losing Donte DiVincenzo to a ruptured Achilles tendon and seeing both All-NBA mainstay Anthony Edwards and Denver series folk hero Ayo Dosunmu suffer injuries could be considered something of a success. But that was not the lens through which Tim Connelly saw the team he built once again fall short of the NBA Finals.

"We know our competition is not going to sit still, and nor will we," Minnesota's president of basketball operations told reporters after the season. "If we mess up, we'll mess up loudly. We're going to try to be as aggressive as possible."

You have to give Connelly this much: "loud," "aggressive," "unable to sit still" and "potential for messing up" all certainly feel like prospective descriptors for the play-style of the high-priced, high-wattage, high-wire point guard for whom he so boldly swung this summer .

Betting big on Ball carries risk, both in the combination of high cost ( three years and $130.7 million remaining on the maximum-salaried extension he signed in 2023 ) and low availability due to persistent ankle issues (he's played more than 51 games just twice in six pro seasons) that led the Hornets to look to move him in the first place, and the oft-derided showman's approach to facilitation that can sometimes seem to careen from carefree to careless. In a recent conversation with Britt Robson of MinnPost , Wolves head coach Chris Finch referenced the need for "some redistribution" of Ball's shot selection, which has produced one of the lowest true shooting percentages of any high-usage player in the NBA since his arrival in 2020.

Ball's freewheeling nature could also provide plenty of benefits, though. The Wolves clearly and desperately needed an answer at point guard, another source of shot creation besides superstar guard Anthony Edwards, a ball-handler capable of making opponents pay for double-teaming and trapping the ball out of Edwards' hands, more 3-point shooting, and someone capable of getting the rest of the Wolves — including Ant — higher-quality looks. At his best, Ball ticks every last one of those boxes.

The Hornets scored a scorching 125 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions in Ball's minutes last season. They posted a 57.2% team effective field-goal percentage with him on the court — a mark that would've ranked third in the NBA for the full season . Nearly every Charlotte player who logged significant minutes with Ball shot demonstrably better with him on the floor ; among 287 dudes to play at least 1,000 minutes last season, Ball finished fourth in assists on 3-pointers per 100 possessions, behind only Giannis Antetokounmpo, Josh Giddey (about whom the Wolves also inquired this summer, according to Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic ) and Isaiah Collier, according to PBP Stats .

While he has not been a particularly efficient scorer himself, Ball has consistently run efficient offenses ; the Hornets were better, often a lot better, with him on the court every year of his career . A cynic might suggest those gaudy on-off splits owe more to the relative lack of talent in Charlotte than to anything inherently special about LaMelo. A more optimistic sort might note that last season, the first time Ball had something like commensurate talent around him, the Hornets finished with a top-five offense and a near-top-10 defense and went 33-16 after Jan. 1 … and were still 9.9 points-per-100 better with LaMelo on the floor than off it .

The Wolves are betting that, even in a new context, Ball can still be that sort of rising tide. They think they'll reap the benefits of allowing Edwards to go back to his more natural off-guard position after his average time of possession, seconds and dribble per touch, and overall on-ball percentage (literally how big a share of your total floor time you have the ball in your hands) have exploded over the past two seasons amid Mike Conley's aging, Rob Dillingham's ineffectiveness and a general paucity of viable point-guard play.

Moreover, they think Ball can boost their offense — a middling 14th last season — not only by reducing Edwards' ball-handling and shot-creation burden, but by creating the sort of advantages that generate more good looks and easy opportunities for others.

"We needed a guy like LaMelo to make everybody better," a Wolves source told Krawczynski after the trade . "That was the thing that was missing."

Jaden McDaniels, fresh off averaging a career-best 14.8 points per game in the regular season and 16.3 points per game in the playoffs, could hang 20 a night given more chances to attack and slice through a coverage that Ball has already compromised. Rudy Gobert stands to benefit immensely from the arrival of a pick-and-roll savant who can not only make every read on the floor, but actually throw a catchable alley-oop to the 7-foot-1 Frenchman. Ball's predilection toward pace-pushing and hit-ahead passing could unleash newly minted power forward Jonathan Kuminga, and potentially unlock more fast-break opportunities for an offense that has gotten out in transition at middle-of-the-pack-or-worse rates in each of the last four seasons .

Along with all the excitement surrounding how LaMelo can supercharge Minnesota's offense, questions still abound. How effectively will Edwards and Ball mesh? After being the centerpiece in Charlotte for a half-dozen years, will LaMelo struggle to defer to a peer that is both more richly decorated with individual and team success and firmly ensconced as the face of the franchise? (That the two stars were reportedly working out together in Minnesota for most of August seems like a promising start.)

Can Minnesota's medical and training staff succeed where Charlotte's struggled in keeping Ball on the floor? Is the 2025-26 campaign, which saw Ball play 72 games and 2,017 minutes, more likely to repeat than the previous three, which saw him play an average of 35 games and 1,161 minutes ? How well can Gobert, McDaniels, Edwards and Co. insulate Ball on the other end of the floor, where Finch acknowledged to Robson that the Wolves will "have to build a defense around helping him?" And after playing a grand total of zero postseason games through six professional seasons — and having his fair share of shaky moments in Charlotte's multiple play-in tournament appearances — is Ball ready for the quantum leap in operational duties required of the primary ball-handler and table-setter of a team that harbors legitimate championship aspirations?

"We think the sky is the limit with his game," Connelly told reporters in July . "When he's healthy, there's not more than a handful of more impactful guys on winning in the NBA."

If Connelly's right, the reconstituted Wolves may well have the firepower to be able to stare down the likes of Oklahoma City and San Antonio without blinking come springtime. And if he's not … well, if nothing else, they'll have messed up loudly.

Jaylen Brown , whose fit in Philly should be fascinating, and could be fantastic; Paul George and Mitchell Robinson , who have to stay healthy to make the Celtics' post-Jays pivot stand up; Naz Reid , stepping into a starting spot in Charlotte; Marcus Smart , who should be nails in Houston ; Luguentz Dort , whose arrival could make the Hawks a snarling defensive team with real offensive questions; Julius Randle , getting a second opportunity to be a floor-raising franchise-changer in New York (albeit in a different borough this time); Tyler Herro , now the highest-paid player and highest-profile guard on a Bucks team built to be torn down; Peyton Watson , a gamble the Cavs really need to pay off; Ben Simmons , starting over at age 30 in Sacramento.

articles.title: Stephen Curry Hints at Taking Discount in Warriors Contract amid 'Absolute Desperation to Win'
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry is desperate for another title before he retires, and he's willing to sacrifice financially to get it.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry is desperate for another title before he retires, and he's willing to sacrifice financially to get it.

Amid contract talks with the Warriors, Curry said he's willing to take a discount to help the front office build a competitive roster.

"We're in a very interesting situation," Curry told ESPN's Anthony Slater . "All the different salary cap conditions of whether I sign for a max or less or whatever it is, I want to be on a competitive team. I want to have an opportunity to have some flexibility because we haven't had that in years past, the recent past.

Steph Reveals 'Crazy' Injury During Dynasty

"… This team should have flexibility to make necessary moves if things happen. Those are always just the considerations. For me, information and patience is key. It's just a very unique situation all the way around based on where we've been the last four years, where I'm at in my career, what our team looks like this year and the absolute desperation to win. Trying to balance all that."

Curry, 38, is currently set to play the 2026-27 campaign on a one-year, $62.6 million expiring deal. According to Slater, the Warriors have given him several options, including a max deal or smaller pay cuts. The team has also given him the option to wait and decide later this year or next offseason.

Slater noted that Curry has weighed his options for almost a month, but has not yet made a decision heading into the start of preseason practice next week.

"It's going to happen at the right time, once I have all the information I need to make the decision that is right," Curry said. "The team's been great having that conversation back and forth. If I don't sign, it won't affect me in terms of my play or carrying that weight. But I'll make the decision when I'm ready."

While Curry might be past his prime, he's earned the right to command a max-level deal after all the success he's brought to the organization. He's also still managed to stay productive, putting up 26.6 points per game last year, though he played just 43 contests.

But at this point in his career, it's fair to assume Curry values winning over money.

Golden State missed out on landing players like LeBron James, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Jaylen Brown this offseason, but the team is set up to potentially make some key signings next summer.

The Warriors are projected to have more than $100 million in cap space next offseason, per Spotrac . If Curry opts for a cheaper deal, they could use that money to build a championship roster around him.

As it stands now, the 2027 free agent class is expected to be a loaded one with names like Kevin Durant, Anthony Davis, Karl-Anthony Towns, Kyrie Irving and potentially more.

articles.title: Juancho: "Antes de fichar por el Panathinaikos, mi hermano me llamaba para ir al Barcelona"
articles.standfirst: El jugador del Panathinaikos, gran protagonista de Euroleague & Friends Made in Spain, el podcast de la Euroliga en español en colaboración con MARCA
articles.summary: El jugador del Panathinaikos, gran protagonista de Euroleague & Friends Made in Spain, el podcast de la Euroliga en español en colaboración con MARCA
articles.body: Comenzó oficialmente la segunda temporada de 'Euroleague & Friends Made in Spain', el podcast de la Euroliga en español en colaboración con MARCA que conducen brillantemente Javier Gancedo y Quino Colom y en el que siemrpe tratan de entrevistar a un jugador o entrenador español influyente en la Euroliga desde un punto de vista muy distendido, casi como una charla entre amigos. En esta ocasión y para celebrar el arranque de una nueva edición, tras el enorme éxito de la primera, el podcast y todo el equipo se trasladó a Atenas para hablar nada menos que con Juancho Hernangómez, un jugador tremendamente querido en la capital griega y considerado un héroe en el equipo verde de Atenas. Ante una nueva temporada que arranca este jueves y con el Panathinaikos instalado entre los grandes favoritos, Juancho se convierte en uno de los focos principales de la competición. Con Gancedo y Colom, con el que coincidió en el Estudiantes y en la selección que ganó el Mundial 2019, habló de muchos temas deportivos y no deportivos y contó algunas anécdotas imperdibles. "Quino ha sido uno de los mejores veteranos que he tenido en mi vida. me enseñó mucho y me cuidó como un hermano pequeño, quedándose conmigo siempre a tirar o invitándome a cenar y a todo. Eso me quedó porque ahora soy yo el que invito a los pequeños por el hecho de ayudarles y enseñarles". "En las Ventanas no logramos el objetivo, pero fue una buena lección para todos y en especial para los más jóvenes que vienen muy fuertes con mucho talento y mucha hambre y el futuro de España está garantizado con ellos". "Tengo muchas ganas de apender de Zeljko (Obradovic). Yo he sido siempre un jugador que me ha gustado ser entrenado, de que un entrtenador pueda sacar la mejor versión de mi. Tengo muchas expectativas con Zeljko. Llevamos dos semanas y es un cambio de filosofía completo". "Estaba en mi casa haciendo la maleta con Xavi Rabaseda. Y tenía unas Kobe doradas que me encantaban y cuando las cogí tuve un 'feeling' especial con ellas. Y según las metí en la maleta le digo a Xavi 'mira, estas para la final'. Vamos pasando fases y nos metemos en la final. Pero en la sesión de tiro antes del partido me las pongo y me hacen ampollas y me crean dolor. Así que en la final, cuando estaba a punto de terminar el partido, le pido a un utillero que me las traiga y fui donde estaba Kobe para pedir que me las firmara. Fui el niño más feliz del mundo". "En Berlín gané el Eurobasket y la Euroliga. Allí no he perdido ni un partido. Y encima las chicas acaban de ganar ahí el bronce Mundial". Feliz en Atenas "Estoy muy feliz en Atenas. Desde el primer día que me recibieron 15.000 aficionados con bengalas y pensé ¿dónde me he metido?. ¿Por qué no firmo en España y estoy tranquilo? Pero siempre me han gustado los caminos más difíciles y locos". "Camino del pabellón tras mi llegada, ibamos en la furgoneta y ya habíamos pasado a los aficionados del PAO y de repente cayó algo en el parabrisas y era un pollo sin cabeza. Uno de los de seguridad dijo 'esos son del Olympiacos'. En ese momento estaba acojonado. Aquí es imposible pasar desapercibido". "Con mi mejor amigo del equipo estos tres años que es Jerian Grant, hablamos de que en cuatro o cinco años nadie nos pedirá fotos, que se nos acabará esta vida. Por eso hay que disfrutarla". "Con Jokic tuve una gran relación y sigo en contacto con él. Jugar a su lado es muy fácil, es como hacerlo con Marc o Ricky, o Quino, es decir que te ayudan y que generan para ti. Es una gran persona y muy humilde". "Los 10 partidos que jugué en Minnesota fueron probablemente los mejores que jugué en la NBA y me ayudaron a firmar el gran contrato, el segundo, que firmé después. Era feliz porque de alguna manera apostaban por mí, jugando muchos minutos. Y tras jugar contra Houston y meter 18 puntos, me encontré con una noticia que decía: la NBA suspendida. Luego hubo varios meses en los que no sabíamos que iba a pasar". "Donde más feliz he estado jugando al baloncesto es aquí estos tres años. Compitiendo, ganado títulos buscando un rol importante. Antes de fichar por el Panathiniakos mi hermano, que estaba en Barcelona, me llamaba a diario para que fichara por el Barça. Tenía muchas ofertas, el Madrid estaba pendiente, también el Maccabi o el Fenerbahce. Todos los equipos. Fue una decisión difícil pero muy personal". "Dimitris Giannakopoulos es, rebelde sí, pero sobre todo porque siempre quiere ganar y por eso ha tenido éxito en sus negocios. Sus trabajadores dicen que es el mejor jefe que han tenido, que siempre está pendiente de ti. Es muy cariñoso, pero es el dueño de un equipo que quiere ganar". "El problema de las redes es que hay gente joven que piensa que eso es la realidad, me da pena por ellos. En las redes se ve que alguien siempre está feliz, sin problemas y no es la realidad. Me apena que la gente joven crezca con eso y con la idea de que si no alcanza ese estatus, de belleza, de moda o lo que sea, piensen que no lo han conseguido". "Los hijos de Jerian Grant son como mis hijos. Esa es la familia del Panathiniakos, que como todas tienen problemas. Pero queremos ganar aquí como familila. Y eso es algo que he visto en estos tres años y Giannakopoulos está consiguiendo que sea cada vez más importante". "Se vive de una manera jugando en casa y otra jugando fuera. Pero me gusta mucho jugarlos. Al final nos jugamos casi todos los títulos contra ellos, igual jugamos contra ellos 15 o 20 veces al año. Cuado jugamos en casa no hay ningún aficionado del Olympiacos y cuando vamos allí no hay ningún aficionado nuestro. Hay mucha tensión y presión y cada cosa puede ser viral. Y pase lo que pase, el final del partido se va a liar. Que se cruce la línea deportiva, no me gusta. Hay que demostrarlo en el campo". Una final Panathinaikos - Oympiacos "El año pasado casi todo el mundo la deseaba por ser en el OAKA, pero al final de quererla tanto no salió, no llegamos y el Valencia se lo mereció. El Olympiacos ganó en nuestra casa y eso para el aficionado del Panathinaikos es un sufrmiento, el día más negro de su vida".

articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers are gearing up for training camp, just like everyone else around the NBA. LA finds itself in a little bit of a roster dilemma, as the team will have to make some moves before the 15-man roster is announced.

The team currently has one player over the allowed amount, and there are three players who are in danger of being waived from the roster.

"Clearly, the Lakers need to dump someone, and I think it's going to be one of three players," Lakers insider Jovan Buha said. "It's going to either be Dalton Knecht , Jaden Hardy , or Bronny James."

The Lakers still have some question marks left to be answered. One of the biggest is the power forward position and overall big-man depth. They are still in the market for someone who can help in the frontcourt.

"The Lakers are still monitoring the market for big men, team sources told The Athletic," The Athletic's Dan Woike reported. "They traded for Walker Kessler and signed Kevon Looney to play center, and Mamukelashvili can play the position, too. The team could address the position either by trade or signing, like with potentially adding Thybulle. The roster is currently at full capacity."

Bleacher Report's Eric Pincus has named Julius Randle as someone LA should consider trading for.

"Still, if he's available, Randle would give the Lakers a very different frontcourt alongside Kessler, with Mamukelashvili backing him up. The Timberwolves sent him to the Brooklyn Nets this summer in the LaMelo Ball blockbuster. Randle doesn't fit the Nets' timeline, and while they probably won't deal him before the season starts, he's definitely a player to watch ahead of the trade deadline. Randle is expensive at $33.3 million. The Lakers would need to include LaRavia , Hardy, Knecht, and Vanderbilt," Pincus wrote.

There is nothing like a blockbuster trade to set the NBA off at some point. The good news for the Lakers is that they would be getting off contracts they already really don't want to keep.

Randle has made $195 million throughout his career thus far. He is a bully inside the paint and has developed a smooth shot from beyond the arc. This is the type of deal the Lakers could look to make sooner rather than later.

articles.title: LeBron James bought a $2.1 million Akron property at 18; over two decades later, his 30,000-square-foot mansion is valued at nearly $10 million
articles.summary: LeBron James has turned a childhood dream into a real estate story that stretches far beyond basketball.
articles.body: LeBron James has turned a childhood dream into a real estate story that stretches far beyond basketball. The Akron property he purchased at just 18 has become one of the most talked-about parts of his life off the court. What began as a major investment for a young NBA rookie now stands as a symbol of his long connection to his hometown, his rise to global fame, and the wealth he has built over two decades. The mansion’s reported value, nearing $10 million, adds another chapter to James’ remarkable journey.LeBron James’ Akron mansion began with a $2.1 million purchaseIn 2003, LeBron James entered the NBA as the Cleveland Cavaliers’ No. 1 overall pick. He was only 18, but his life was already changing at a pace few teenagers could imagine. Soon after the draft, the Akron native purchased a property in Bath Township, near the city where he grew up, for a reported $2.1 million.The purchase marked an early step into property ownership for a player whose professional career had barely begun. But James did not simply settle into the existing house. He eventually had it demolished and replaced it with a custom-built mansion designed to meet his family’s needs and reflect his growing success.The new residence took shape over the following years. Reports place the completion of the expansive home around 2007, transforming the original property into a sprawling private estate. The distinction matters: the widely reported $2.1 million figure refers to the initial property purchase, not the total cost of the mansion as it stands today.Inside LeBron James’ 30,000-square-foot Akron mansionThe scale of James’ Akron home is striking even by celebrity real estate standards. The mansion reportedly spans about 30,000 square feet and sits on roughly seven acres. It includes six bedrooms, eight full bathrooms and six half-bathrooms, creating ample space for family life, guests and entertainment.Its amenities go well beyond the basics. The property features a two-lane bowling alley, a home theater, a recording studio, an aquarium and a sports bar. A private barbershop adds another unusual touch, while the primary suite reportedly includes a two-story walk-in closet.These features offer a glimpse into how the estate blends comfort with recreation. Rather than functioning only as a place to sleep between NBA seasons, the house can accommodate a range of activities without requiring its residents to leave the property.The size and custom features also help explain why the home’s reported value is far removed from the price James paid for the original property. Still, its market value should not be confused with a guaranteed sale price. A reported estimate of around $9.2 million to $10 million is not the same as a recent independent appraisal or a completed transaction.How LeBron James’ Akron property reached a reported $10 million valueMore than two decades after the initial purchase, LeBron James’ Akron estate is commonly estimated to be worth close to $10 million. That figure reflects the scale of the finished property, its land and its location, rather than a simple increase in the value of the original purchase.The distinction is important. James demolished the existing house, built a much larger residence and expanded the property over time. Reports also note that he purchased nearby parcels in later years. Those additional investments, along with construction costs, taxes, upkeep and other expenses, would all affect the true financial picture.As a result, comparing the initial $2.1 million purchase with today’s estimated value does not provide a complete measure of profit. The mansion has certainly become a high-value asset, but the total amount James invested in creating and maintaining it is not fully captured by those two figures.The estate is also part of a wider real estate portfolio that has included homes in Miami and Los Angeles. His moves across the NBA have brought new properties and changing living arrangements, yet the Akron compound has remained a constant in his property story.Why LeBron James has held on to his Akron homeLeBron James’ continued ownership of the Akron estate carries meaning beyond its estimated price. He grew up in the city and rose to national prominence while playing high school basketball at St. Vincent-St. Mary. His hometown remains closely tied to his public identity, even as his career has taken him to different cities.The mansion also stands apart from the more recent homes associated with his time in California. It represents an early milestone, purchased at the beginning of a career that would eventually make him one of the most successful athletes in the world.LebrJames’ connection to Akron extends beyond real estate. Through the LeBron James Family Foundation, he has invested in local initiatives, including the I PROMISE School and community-focused projects. Those efforts form part of a broader relationship with the city that helped shape his life.The Akron property’s estimated value may attract attention, but its significance cannot be measured by square footage or dollars alone.
